title: Urban climate dynamics in informal settlements: Spatiotemporal rainfall and temperature variability in Thembelihle, Johannesburg
content:
by Sailas Hussein Matamanda, Walter Musakwa, Armstrong Dzomba

Climate change has emerged as a critical contemporary concern, marked by greater variability and severity in weather systems, from extreme heat to drought and intense precipitation. Africa is particularly vulnerable, with urban settlements facing disproportionate risks. This study investigates long-term temperature and rainfall dynamics in Thembelihle, an informal settlement in Johannesburg, alongside broader metropolitan trends, using robust statistical and geospatial methods. Temperature and rainfall data spanning five decades (1974–2024 for Thembelihle; 1981–2024 for Johannesburg) were examined using the non-parametric Mann-Kendall (MK) Test and Sen’s Slope estimation to detect monotonic trends. Rainfall indices included the number of wet days (NWDT), the highest number of consecutive wet days (HNCWD), the highest number of consecutive dry days (HNCDD), and the maximum daily rainfall (HRPD). Extreme temperature events in Thembelihle were examined using a Peak Over Threshold (POT) approach. Spatial interpolation of CHIRPS rainfall and ERA5 temperature anomalies was conducted in QGIS to visualize spatiotemporal variability across Johannesburg. Results reveal statistically significant warming in Thembelihle, with minimum temperatures increasing at 0.0505 °C/year and maximum temperatures at 0.0391 °C/year, remaining higher than Johannesburg’s anomaly trend, although the magnitude of this difference is reduced when trends are compared over a harmonised temporal baseline (1981–2024). Extreme heat events, though historically rare, have clustered in recent years, signalling emerging instability. Rainfall patterns in Thembelihle show high interannual variability with no significant long-term decline, though spring rainfall exhibits a borderline decreasing trend. Johannesburg’s rainfall metrics highlight intensifying extremes: longer dry spells (+1 day/year) and higher maximum daily rainfall (+0.30 mm/year). Drought analysis identifies overlapping severe years (1984, 1999, 2003), underscoring regional susceptibility, while Thembelihle’s higher variability points to localized vulnerability. Spatial analysis confirms rainfall gradients, with wetter conditions in the northeast and drier conditions in the south, alongside localized temperature hotspots. These findings demonstrate a dual climate challenge: accelerating heat stress and increasingly variable rainfall. Informal settlements such as Thembelihle are disproportionately exposed, requiring both water resource coordination and localized adaptation strategies.
